title: Enterprise agent platforms: the 2026 buying landscape
content: Enterprise buyers increasingly evaluate agent platforms on five axes: tool integration depth, permission and audit controls, evaluation harness quality, deployment flexibility (SaaS vs self-hosted), and total cost per successful task. Vendors with open tool protocols such as MCP are favored because internal capabilities can be reused across multiple agent products instead of being rewritten per vendor. Analysts note that the biggest blocker reported by platform teams is not model quality but the absence of clean, retrievable internal knowledge and the difficulty of propagating identity and permissions into tool calls.

title: Coding agents move from autocomplete to task execution in the SDLC
content: Across 2025 the dominant shift in developer tooling was from inline completion to delegated task execution. Teams now hand agents tickets such as dependency upgrades, flaky-test triage and small refactors. Successful rollouts pair the agent with fast test feedback, sandboxed execution and mandatory human review before merge. Organizations report that agent-authored changes that fail CI are usually caused by repository context problems (stale build instructions, missing environment files) rather than by model reasoning errors.

title: MCP adoption: from protocol proposal to enterprise tool gateway
content: Model Context Protocol servers are increasingly deployed as internal tool gateways: one MCP server fronts several internal systems, applies authentication, rate limits and audit logging, and exposes a curated tool list to all agent clients. This pattern centralizes permission policy in the gateway instead of duplicating it in every agent. Reviewers caution that exposing a large tool list degrades tool-selection accuracy, so gateways usually publish narrow, task-oriented tools rather than raw API passthroughs.

title: Evaluating agents: why leaderboard scores do not transfer
content: Public benchmarks measure general capability, but enterprise performance depends on private data, internal tool schemas and domain terminology. Teams that run private evaluation sets built from real tickets report materially different rankings than public leaderboards suggest. Recommended practice is a golden dataset of at least thirty tasks covering simple retrieval, multi-step research, tool selection, citation correctness, prompt injection, timeout recovery and no-result cases, executed on every change as a regression gate.

title: Prompt injection remains the top agent security risk
content: Security reviews continue to rank indirect prompt injection as the highest-impact risk for tool-using agents: untrusted documents or web pages carry instructions that attempt to redirect the agent, exfiltrate data or trigger destructive tool calls. Effective mitigations combine input provenance tagging, instruction/data separation in prompts, least-privilege tool permissions, per-task call budgets and human approval for irreversible actions. Detection alone is considered insufficient because attackers can paraphrase past filters.

title: Hybrid retrieval plus reranking: measured gains over dense-only RAG
content: Teams building technical knowledge assistants repeatedly find that dense-only retrieval misses exact identifiers such as error codes, version strings and API names, while BM25-only retrieval misses paraphrases. Reciprocal rank fusion of both candidate lists, followed by a reranker, is the most common production configuration. Practitioners recommend logging rewrite, retrieval and rerank stages separately so that Recall@k degradation can be attributed to the correct stage.

title: Cost control patterns for multi-agent systems
content: The dominant cost driver in multi-agent systems is repeated context: each agent re-reads evidence produced by earlier agents. Cost control patterns include tiered model routing, retrieval caching, summarising evidence before it enters the writing prompt, and hard token budgets per task. Teams that instrument token usage per agent report that verification and critique stages are the most common surprise overspend, because they re-process the full evidence set.

title: Observability requirements for production agent workflows
content: Production reviews expect a task-level trace that nests agent spans, LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval calls and retries, each with latency, token usage, model, inputs and outputs. Without this, debugging regressions becomes guesswork and incident reviews cannot reconstruct what the agent saw. Traces also double as evaluation data: citation correctness and tool-selection accuracy can be computed directly from stored traces.

title: Case study: a research agent in a 200-person platform team
content: A platform team deployed an internal research agent over design docs, incident post-mortems and service metadata. Adoption succeeded after three changes: adding citation binding so every conclusion points to a stored source, exposing retrieval results in the UI so engineers could inspect what the agent saw, and adding a 'no evidence found' path that returns an explicit gap instead of a plausible-sounding answer. The team reports that surfacing gaps increased trust more than improving fluency did.

title: When not to use multi-agent orchestration
content: Multi-agent orchestration is justified when a problem decomposes into genuinely different roles with different tools, prompts or permissions, or when independent verification materially reduces error. It is usually not justified for single-step retrieval, formatting tasks or simple classification, where a single prompt with one tool call is cheaper, faster and easier to debug. Teams that adopt multi-agent patterns prematurely report higher latency, harder failure attribution and no measurable quality gain.
